clue.text: Change arrangements as green beret essentially opens burst of gunfire

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only the centre of beret is kept
a burst scatters things, so the letters of gunfire are blown apart and regrouped

blocks.note: the middle letter of this five-letter word
eco- is the environmentally green prefix

explanation.surface: A green-bereted commando's burst of gunfire forces a change of plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opens' says the green-beret letters come first; the setter puts the core of beret ahead of ECO to make RECO, then the shuffled gunfire gives RECONFIGURE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reconfigure is to set something up in a new way, i.e. alter its arrangement.

clue.text: Crew maybe worried in audition

indicators.note: an audition is a hearing, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: 'what's eating you?' – to eat someone is to worry them, so worried is ate

explanation.surface: A crew member is anxious at an audition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' is a rowing crew; an eight is the standard eight-oared racing boat and its rowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowing eight is one example of a crew, hence the 'maybe' in the clue.

clue.text: I ruined only chance

blocks.note: the Roman numeral I is one
something shot is wrecked or done for

explanation.surface: Someone laments that they have blown their only chance.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-shot opportunity is a single attempt with no second go.

clue.text: Admit free schools extremely well-informed

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters, applied to both free and schools

blocks.note: to be up on a subject is to know it well

explanation.surface: A policy line: allow free schools in, being thoroughly knowledgeable.
explanation.definitionFit: To fess up is an informal phrasal verb for confessing, owning up to something.

clue.text: Station wagon in middle – a Ford that doesn't start

indicators.note: asks for the single central letter of wagon
a name that does not start has lost its opening letter

explanation.surface: A car buyer wants a mid-range estate, a Ford that won't start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Station wagon' and 'Ford' read as cars; Ford is the actor Harrison Ford, whose first name loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To garrison a place is to station troops there, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Irritated Republicans seeing Democrats on other side of joint

blocks.note: the ankle is a joint of the leg
D abbreviates Democrat, placed on the far side of the joint

explanation.surface: US politics: Republicans annoyed to find Democrats across the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that rankled caused lasting resentment and annoyance.

clue.text: Perhaps Quasimodo's sort of almost coping without Esmerelda in the end

indicators.note: the end of a name is its final letter, so only the last letter of Esmerelda is wanted
to sort letters is to put them in a fresh order

blocks.note: her final letter, set outside the rest

explanation.surface: The bell-ringer of Notre-Dame barely managing without his beloved Esmeralda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' looks like an instruction to cut coping, but it is fodder itself; 'without' means outside, adding the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Quasimodo is the bell-ringer in Hugo's novel, and a campanologist is a bell-ringer.

clue.text: Unreasonable American boxer possibly holding on to Greek character

indicators.note: to hold on to something is to keep it within your grip

blocks.note: a female boxer dog, among other breeds, is a bitch
mu is the twelfth Greek letter

explanation.surface: An American fighter clinging to a Greek opponent is being unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxer is a dog breed, not a fighter, and a female dog is a bitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is a bit much is an idiom for calling it excessive or unfair.

clue.text: Airlines charge for this rest day after going on vacation, BA included

indicators.note: after says the piece for day is placed second, behind the piece for going
a vacated house is emptied, so going keeps only its outside letters
something included is set inside, so the airline's initials go into the middle

blocks.note: the rest, what remains over, is the excess
the word emptied of its interior
'in my day' – a day is an era or age

explanation.surface: A traveller resting a day after a holiday flight with British Airways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rest' here is the noun for what is left over, not a break; 'day' as in 'in my day' means an era. BA is the airline British Airways.
explanation.definitionFit: Airlines levy a fee for luggage over the free weight allowance, which is excess baggage.

clue.text: Row river to keep fit – quite the reverse

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside; 'quite the reverse' says it is the fit that holds the river

blocks.note: an ague is a feverish shivering fit

explanation.surface: An instruction to row on the river to stay fit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as written, the river would hold the fit; 'quite the reverse' swaps the roles so AGUE holds R.
explanation.definitionFit: A row (rhyming with cow) is a quarrel, and to argue is to have one.

clue.text: Hot buffet is safe

blocks.note: to buffet is to strike, to box

explanation.surface: A reassurance that the warm buffet food is fine to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buffet' suggests a meal, but here it is the verb meaning to strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A strongbox is a lockable metal container for valuables, which is a safe.

clue.text: When discounted chipolatas must be cooked with posh oil?

indicators.note: a discounted item has had a portion taken off it
cooking transforms ingredients, so the remaining letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: as and when both mean at the time that

explanation.surface: Kitchen talk: cut-price sausages need frying in fancy oil.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove AS from CHIPOLATAS, leaving CHIPOLAT, then shuffle it together with U. A chipolata is a thin British sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: Patchouli is an aromatic essential oil from an Asian plant, used in perfumes.

clue.text: Turner having time for hot drink

indicators.note: 'X for Y' means X takes the place of Y, swapping one letter in

blocks.note: a lathe turns wood or metal
H abbreviates hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: The painter Turner taking a break for a warm drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner looks like the painter J.M.W. Turner, but it is a machine that turns; T replaces the H in LATHE.
explanation.definitionFit: A latte is a coffee made with lots of steamed milk, a hot drink.

clue.text: Almost steal Jaguar with vacuous police missing degree of precision

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of steal's synonym goes
vacuous means empty, so police is stripped of its insides
the car's name is missing the emptied police letters

blocks.note: to nick is British slang for to steal

explanation.surface: A car thief nearly gets away with a Jaguar when the dim police fail to show.
explanation.walkthrough: NICK loses its K; E-TYPE loses the P and E that remain of empty police, leaving ETY.
explanation.definitionFit: A nicety is a fine detail or subtle distinction, a matter of exactness.

clue.text: Prisoners order case of minestrone soup?

indicators.note: a case is the outside wrapping, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: OM is the Order of Merit

explanation.surface: Inmates request a bowl of minestrone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' is not a request but an honour: the Order of Merit, abbreviated OM.
explanation.definitionFit: Consommé is a clear soup made from concentrated stock.

clue.text: Some find old rum smugglers' ships becalmed here?

indicators.note: 'some' points to part of the following words, a run of letters taken from inside them

blocks.note: spans the end of find through the start of smugglers'

explanation.surface: Searching for old rum-runners' ships stuck without wind.
explanation.definitionFit: The doldrums are the calm equatorial belt where sailing ships were often left without wind.

clue.text: Concert books initially embarrassed Ronnie Barker

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the two words that follow

blocks.note: a Prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms

explanation.surface: A concert where the comedian Ronnie Barker was embarrassed by bookings.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie Barker was a British comedian, but the definition is just 'Barker'.
explanation.definitionFit: A barker drums up business outside a show by calling to passers-by, promoting it.

clue.text: Lighthouse, say, after both sides of lamp-room fitted with high-water survival equipment

indicators.note: the two sides of a word are its first and last letters
something fitted is installed inside, so the next piece goes between the two sides

blocks.note: with and and both join things

explanation.surface: A lighthouse's lamp-room kitted out with flood survival gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' gives its synonym rather than acting as a joining word, and the high-water equipment is Noah's.
explanation.definitionFit: A lighthouse is an example of a landmark, a prominent feature used for finding the way.

clue.text: Is this king working to stop protest?

indicators.note: a stopper plugs the inside of something, so this piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the king is trying to halt a demonstration.
explanation.definitionFit: A king is one type of monarch, a hereditary sovereign ruler.

clue.text: A sort of maths condition

indicators.note: sorting things means putting them in another order

explanation.surface: A sort of maths condition, as though fear of numbers were a disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma is a respiratory medical condition causing breathing difficulty.

clue.text: On reflection I made a mistake about hotel with a male cleaner

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front
about means surrounding, so the exclamation goes round the next pieces

blocks.note: the exclamation when you slip up
H is hotel in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A hotel guest admits an error about a male cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: SPOO wraps round HAM after its first letter: S-HAM-POO.
explanation.definitionFit: Shampoo is a liquid soap for washing hair or carpets, a cleaning agent.

clue.text: Steep, and Dawn French is wanting flatter cycling

indicators.note: cycling means rotating, so the first letter of flatter's synonym moves to the end
wanting means lacking, so those letters are taken out of the name

blocks.note: the British comedian, taken as written
to fawn is to flatter obsequiously

explanation.surface: Dawn French, the comedian, looks for a less hilly bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Dawn French is a British comic actress; 'cycling' is not about bikes but rotates the letters of the synonym before they are removed from her name.
explanation.definitionFit: To steep something is to soak it in liquid, which is to drench it.

clue.text: Adult daughter finally wearing dress

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the word
the wearer is inside the clothing, so this letter goes within

blocks.note: a gown is a long dress

explanation.surface: A grown-up daughter finally putting on a frock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daughter' tempts as D; here only its last letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Grown, as in a grown man, is an adjective meaning fully mature.

clue.text: Helping to build a wall … or knocking one down?

blocks.note: first meaning: laying bricks with lime and sand paste
second meaning: bombarding with a short-barrelled artillery gun

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis and question mark set builder against destroyer; both are the same word from two different nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortar is both the bricklayer's bonding paste and a high-angle gun, and each gives a verb.

clue.text: Smooths horsehair on some trousers

indicators.note: read as a verb, trousers means pockets or holds, so the phrase before it holds the word

blocks.note: spans the end of horsehair, all of on, and the start of some

explanation.surface: Someone pressing horsehair off a pair of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' looks like the garment, but is the verb meaning pockets.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron is to press fabric flat with a hot iron, making it smooth.

clue.text: Seen to embody merit – making every scheme ultimately a benevolent one

indicators.note: to embody is to take something into a body, so one word holds the other
every instance of the last letter of scheme is to be turned into a different letter

explanation.surface: Being visibly deserving makes every plan, in the end, a good deed.
explanation.walkthrough: SE(MERIT)EN has four Es; turning every one into A gives SA(MARIT)AN.
explanation.definitionFit: From the parable of the Good Samaritan, a samaritan is a kindly person who helps others.

clue.text: Spike Milligan's back on for good

indicators.note: the back of a name is its final letter

explanation.surface: Spike Milligan's comeback, this time for good.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan was a British comedian of The Goon Show; 'Spike' is lifted off his name to be the definition. His final N goes on PRO, then G.
explanation.definitionFit: A prong is a pointed tine, as on a fork, which is a spike.

clue.text: Typically broke one font's setting with computer equipment

blocks.note: a baptismal font stands in a church

explanation.surface: A computer setup broke a printing typeface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'font' suggests typography; it is the basin for baptisms.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'poor as a church mouse' makes this creature the proverbial example of being penniless.
